3 years in strategy consulting at ZS Associates — plus some independent ventures along the way.

Strategy consultant, currently pursuing a postgraduate program in technology and business management at Masters' Union. This site is less a resume and more a closer look at how I think — the questions I ask, the work I've done, and what I pay attention to beyond the job description.

How I think

Most strategy problems arrive unlabeled — a vague ask, stakeholders who each see the problem differently, and more opinions than data. My work usually starts one step before the actual problem: figuring out what the real question is.

Click any stage above to see how it played out in practice.

In practice

On one project, a client's specialist internal team felt disconnected from the rest of the business, and both sides had reasons to explain why. The real question wasn't how to get that team more resources — it was understanding why its value wasn't visible to the people it worked with. Everything else followed from getting that right.

In practice

On another project, a client's 23 regional teams each used different definitions for the same core metrics, different reporting habits, and had different reasons for resisting a shared standard. Before proposing anything, we had to separate what was genuinely a data problem from what was actually a trust problem.

In practice

Back on the first project: neither side was dismissing the other out of ill intent — they simply didn't see the value each brought to the other. Once that became visible, the tension eased across the organization, without needing to convince each team individually.

In practice

On a third project, redesigning roughly 90 roles across a client's organization in three weeks meant every recommendation had to be immediately actionable — not directionally correct, but specific enough to say who does what, starting Monday.

Work

Three engagements from three years in pharmaceutical strategy consulting at ZS Associates — presented as what actually happened, not what went in the client deck.

Replaced 20+ inconsistent local reporting standards with one regional cadence, across a year-long $1M engagement.

Question

How do you get 23 country teams to report the same way, when none of them asked for it?

The mess

Country leads didn't want to be told how to run things differently. This was fundamentally a change management problem, not a data problem.

My role

Drove planning and execution within a 5-person team on a year-long, ~$1M engagement, run remotely from India.

Approach

Weekly leadership calls to keep everyone informed and heard, one-on-ones with country leads when something looked off, and workshops designed to ensure the recommendations were actually adopted, not just approved in a meeting.

Insight

Securing sign-off was the easy part. Getting people to actually change how they worked required a year of consistent engagement, not a single persuasive presentation.

Output

A single data standard and monthly reporting cadence reviewed directly by regional leadership, replacing 20+ inconsistent local definitions.

Lesson

Patience, in this context, wasn't passive — it was a deliberate plan sustained even when progress wasn't yet visible.

Aligned 10+ senior leaders across functions on Medical Affairs' value to the wider organization.

Question

Why did Medical Affairs feel disconnected from the rest of the company?

The mess

No one could clearly articulate the actual problem — including those closest to it. We had to uncover it ourselves through interviews across every function.

My role

Ran day-to-day execution within a 7-person team spanning India and the US on this repositioning effort.

Approach

Interviewed leaders across commercial, scientific, and medical functions until a clear pattern emerged: each team consistently underestimated what the others contributed.

Insight

The resistance wasn't attributable to any single department. It eased repeatedly, across different teams, once each understood what the others needed from them.

Output

Alignment across 10+ senior leaders on how existing Medical Affairs capabilities could support commercial and scientific priorities.

Lesson

Most alignment problems are, at their core, information problems. Teams aren't opposed to one another — they simply lack visibility into what the other side is managing.

Redesigned ~90 roles across 4 indications in three weeks, without breaking existing relationships.

Question

How do you redesign ~90 people's roles in three weeks without breaking what's already working?

The mess

A three-week timeline, real roles, and real consequences. Every decision affected someone's territory, relationships, or position.

My role

Owned the redesign of a ~90-FTE Medical Affairs organization across 4 indications under a compressed timeline.

Approach

Redesigned territory maps to preserve existing relationships wherever possible, and matched people from shrinking areas into growing ones before defaulting to new hires.

Insight

At that pace, effective delegation isn't optional — without it, mistakes don't just affect you, they cascade to the people you're responsible for.

Output

New territory maps that redeployed up to 8 FTEs from shrinking areas into ones expanding by up to 12, minimizing new hiring.

Lesson

Speed doesn't excuse weak structure — if anything, it demands more discipline, not less.

Journal

Two distinct threads run through this section: a path and a habit. One traces the cities I've deliberately moved to, each a step further from comfort. The other is travel I return to regularly, without any fixed sequence.

The cities I've moved through

In order. Each move was deliberate — into a city where I knew fewer people, by choice.

1

Kerala

Home — where everyone returns to, regardless of where life has taken them.

2

Delhi

Too comfortable. With my parents nearby, I rarely had to take ownership of anything — which is precisely why I chose to leave.

3

Mumbai

Where independence started.

4

Pune

Where independence became tangible — financially and emotionally. This is where the growth actually took shape.

5

Gurgaon

Not for the city itself — a deliberate step toward what's next, while pursuing a PGP at Masters' Union.

Travel, the recurring kind

No fixed order and no destination it's building toward — travel has simply been a consistent habit, roughly quarterly since I started earning, and further back than that. Mostly shot on film: with 36 exposures a roll and a real cost per frame, there's little room to waste shots chasing perfection — only what genuinely felt worth capturing at the time.

Photos and stories in progress. Scope so far: childhood trips to New Zealand, the US, Canada, Malaysia and Hong Kong; self-funded travel since starting work to Vietnam and Turkey; and 20+ Indian states and union territories.
